summary: In this episode, Fathers Andrew Stephen Damick and Stephen De Young discuss the sacrament of holy matrimony within the Orthodox Christian tradition. They begin by examining the creation of humanity in Genesis, emphasizing that humanity is created in the image of God as male and female, which was a radical concept in the ancient world. They explore the meaning of Adam's aloneness, the creation of Eve from Adam's side (not rib), and the foundational principle that marriage is the union of two becoming one flesh. The hosts then trace the theme of marriage through the patriarchal narratives, highlighting Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah as the ideal couple, and Jacob's polygamous struggles. They also discuss the concept of love, contrasting ancient views of love as weakness with Christian love as self-sacrificial action, and critique modern romantic love as consumeristic. The episode moves to the New Testament, examining Christ's teaching on marriage in Matthew 19, St. Paul's instructions in Ephesians 5, and the mystery of marriage as a symbol of Christ and the Church. They also address the historical practice of weddings, debunking the idea that Christians simply adopted Roman civil ceremonies, and instead show how Christian weddings transformed pagan practices. Finally, they explore the theological depth of marriage as a means of theosis, with the Holy Spirit animating the union, and conclude by emphasizing that marriage is not an end in itself but a path to salvation, and that the Church itself is a family, the household of God, which includes all believers.

entities.title: Adam
entities.summary: The first man, created in the image of God, whose aloneness led to the creation of Eve, and whose side was opened to form her.

entities.title: Eve
entities.summary: The first woman, created from Adam's side, becoming his helper and partner, and the mother of all living.

entities.title: Abraham and Sarah
entities.summary: The patriarch and matriarch of Israel, whose marriage is referenced in the Orthodox wedding service, and whose story highlights faithfulness to God and to each other.

entities.title: Isaac and Rebekah
entities.summary: Presented as the ideal married couple in Genesis, their marriage was arranged, yet Isaac loved Rebekah, showing that love is a concrete commitment.

entities.title: Jacob
entities.summary: The patriarch who married Leah and Rachel and had concubines, illustrating the problems of polygamy.

entities.title: Joseph and Asenath
entities.summary: Joseph's marriage to Asenath, a pagan priest's daughter, is expanded in the apocryphal text 'Joseph and Asenath', which portrays her conversion to Judaism.

entities.title: Malachi
entities.summary: The prophet who condemned faithlessness to the wife of youth and declared that God makes husband and wife one with a portion of the Spirit.

entities.title: Jesus Christ
entities.summary: The bridegroom who loves the Church, whose death and resurrection are depicted as a wedding, and who taught on the indissolubility of marriage.

entities.title: St. Paul
entities.summary: The apostle who taught that marriage is a mystery of Christ and the Church, and who gave instructions for husbands and wives.

entities.title: Roman Wedding
entities.summary: The pagan Roman wedding ceremony involved sacrifices to household gods, a fake kidnapping, and a procession, which Christians could not participate in.

entities.title: Orthodox Wedding Service
entities.summary: The Orthodox wedding service references the patriarchal marriages, includes the reading of Ephesians 5, and emphasizes that God joins the couple together.

concepts.title: Image of God
concepts.summary: Humanity is created to bear the image of God, which is not a static quality but a capacity to be exercised in the world, including the distinction of male and female.

concepts.title: One Flesh
concepts.summary: The union of man and woman in marriage, where they become one flesh, is a divine action and the core of marriage, rooted in Genesis and affirmed by Christ.

concepts.title: Christian Love
concepts.summary: Christian love is not a feeling but a concrete action of self-sacrifice and service, directed even to enemies, and is the foundation of marital love.

concepts.title: Mystery of Marriage
concepts.summary: Marriage is a sacrament because it participates in the mystery of Christ and the Church, as stated in Ephesians 5:32, and is a means of theosis.

concepts.title: Bridegroom Imagery
concepts.summary: The Bible frequently uses the imagery of Christ as the bridegroom and the Church as his bride, from the Old Testament prophets to the book of Revelation.

concepts.title: Household of God
concepts.summary: The Church is the household of God, a family where all believers are brothers and sisters, and marriage is about bringing people into this household.

claims.text: The creation of humanity as male and female in Genesis 1 is a radical claim that both sexes bear the image of God equally, which was unique in the ancient world.
The Hebrew and Greek words for 'rib' in Genesis 2 actually mean 'side', indicating that Eve was created from Adam's side, not a rib, and this is a mistranslation.
Marriage is a sacrament because God joins the couple together and gives a portion of the Spirit, as stated in Malachi 2:15, making it a divine action.
Christian love is not a feeling but a concrete action of self-sacrifice, and it is the foundation of marriage, regardless of emotions.
Polygamy is condemned in Scripture, as seen in Leviticus 18:18 and the negative examples of polygamous marriages, and it is not endorsed by the Bible.
Christians did not simply adopt Roman wedding ceremonies, as those were deeply pagan and involved sacrifices to gods, which Christians could not participate in.
Marriage is a means of theosis, as it participates in the mystery of Christ and the Church, and spouses are called to serve each other as Christ serves the Church.
The Church is the household of God, a family where all believers are brothers and sisters, and marriage is about bringing people into this household.

scriptural_links.summary: Humanity is created in the image of God as male and female, establishing the equal dignity of both sexes.
The creation of Eve from Adam's side and the declaration that a man shall leave his parents and cleave to his wife, becoming one flesh.
God makes husband and wife one with a portion of the Spirit, and seeks godly offspring, condemning faithlessness.
Christ quotes Genesis to affirm the indissolubility of marriage and discusses celibacy for the kingdom.
St. Paul calls marriage a profound mystery referring to Christ and the Church.
The consummation of all things is depicted as the wedding feast of the Lamb.

glossary.definition: Hebrew phrase meaning 'helper corresponding to him', indicating a partner who complements and fits together with the man.
Payment made by the groom's family to the bride's family as restitution for taking her from her household, not a purchase of a commodity.
Payment made to the groom along with the bride, often in political marriages, as part of a package.
Gift from the groom to the bride, giving her control over property or money, especially if he dies.
The process of becoming like God through participation in His life, often through the sacraments and faithful living.
In Orthodox theology, a sacrament; an initiation and participation in divine reality, not a puzzle to be solved.
